summary: Gives a perspective on the Host Requirements RFCs, 1122 and 1123, and what went into their development. It is for information only and does not define a protocol.

eli5.summary: A behind-the-scenes look at why the big rule lists for Internet computers turned out the way they did.

questions: why were the host requirements written
what issues did host requirements settle
subtitle: Behind-the-scenes insights into the development of comprehensive Internet host standards.

tldr.problem: Internet host implementations had grown inconsistent and incomplete, with unclear requirements for TCP/IP protocol support, leading to interoperability problems.
tldr.mechanism: The IETF Host Requirements Working Group spent 20 months consolidating and clarifying software requirements for Internet hosts across all protocol layers, producing two major RFCs (1122 and 1123) after extensive technical debate and consensus-building.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1127 explains the working group's decisions, the controversies they faced, and areas left for future work, providing context for implementors and future standards work.

today: RFC 1127 is an informational document providing historical context and analysis. The Host Requirements RFCs (1122 and 1123) that it explains remain foundational standards for Internet host implementation, though updated standards and best practices have evolved since 1989.

sections.title: The Host Requirements Effort
sections.content:
RFC 1127 provides an informal summary of the Host Requirements Working Group's work on defining comprehensive software requirements for Internet hosts. The working group published two major standards documents: RFC 1122 (Requirements for Internet Hosts -- Communication Layers) and RFC 1123 (Requirements for Internet Hosts -- Application and Support).

The effort took 20 months of intensive work, with seven formal meetings and approximately 3 megabytes of email discussion among about 40 Internet experts. The documents went through roughly 20 distinct drafts before reaching consensus. The working group's core goals were interoperability, extensibility, functionality, efficiency, and architectural purity, with interoperability being the highest priority.
sections.eli5: A team of 20-40 Internet experts met regularly for about 20 months to decide and write down all the detailed rules for how computers should run the Internet.

sections.title: What the Host Requirements Cover
sections.content:
The Host Requirements RFCs go far beyond simple prescriptions to include a bibliography of essential documents, corrections and updates to original standards, material filling gaps in specifications, limitations on implementation choices, clarifications of important issues, and documentation of known solutions to recurring problems.

The requirements span all protocol layers: link-layer handling of Ethernet and IEEE 802, network-layer IP behavior including multicasting and source routing, transport-layer TCP and UDP optimizations, and application-layer protocols for mail, file transfer, terminal access, and name resolution. The documents also cover topics like configuration parameters, error logging, and system initialization procedures.
sections.eli5: These standards explain what computers need to do at every level: how to connect to wires, how to send packets across the network, how to reliably talk to each other, and how applications should ask for services.

sections.title: Issues the Working Group Resolved
sections.content:
The working group reached firm consensus on many contentious issues. They required mechanisms to manage and flush outdated ARP cache entries, imposed interoperability requirements for Ethernet and IEEE 802.3, and established many provisions to prevent broadcast storms that could cripple networks.

On TCP, they mandated performance improvements like Van Jacobson's slow-start and congestion-avoidance algorithms, Karn's algorithm for timeout calculation, and TCP window management rules. For DNS, they required hosts to implement the Domain Name System and preferred UDP over TCP for queries. They discouraged source routing of mail for security reasons and required support for multihoming, where a single host has multiple IP addresses.
sections.eli5: The group decided computers must be able to remember network addresses well, prevent messages from overwhelming the network, use fast and smart sending algorithms, find addresses using DNS, and support computers with multiple network connections.

sections.title: Controversial Issues and Disagreements
sections.content:
Some technical issues proved too contentious for consensus. These include whether hosts should forward source-routed datagrams even when not acting as gateways, the correct multihoming model for systems with multiple network interfaces, whether to respond to ICMP Echo Requests directed at broadcast or multicast addresses, and how TCP should handle out-of-order segments.

For other features, the group took compromise positions: they allowed but circumscribed practices like hosts acting as gateways, trailer encapsulation, delayed TCP acknowledgments, and TCP keep-alive mechanisms. The group recognized Jon Postel's Robustness Principle (be conservative in what you send, liberal in what you accept) was sometimes in tension with forward compatibility and security concerns.
sections.eli5: The experts disagreed strongly about a few things: whether computers should forward special routing information, how computers with multiple network connections should work, and how to handle unusual network messages.

sections.title: Issues Deferred for Future Work
sections.content:
The working group identified numerous areas needing future attention. High-priority issues include developing comprehensive host initialization procedures to provide configuration information (like IP addresses and network masks) at boot time, dead gateway detection algorithms that hosts can use to realize a default router has failed, and MTU path discovery to learn the maximum packet size on a particular Internet path.

Other deferred topics include TCP performance guidance (slow-start, congestion avoidance, and the interaction of various algorithms), FTP extensions (atomic store, NDIR commands for directories, adaptive compression), SMTP mail routing standards, and techniques for dynamic DNS discovery and caching. DNS itself needed expansion to incorporate information previously only in the DDN NIC's hosts.txt file.
sections.eli5: The experts left unfinished several important questions about computer startup, detecting failed network equipment, and discovering how big messages can be on a particular path.

sections.title: Impact and Legacy
sections.content:
RFC 1127 illuminates the standards-making process, showing how the working group balanced architectural purity with practical interoperability needs. Many of the requirements documented here were already implicit in original standards but had been violated by real implementations, forcing the group to explicitly restate them.

The document serves as a historical record of host protocol issues as understood in 1989, a snapshot preserved for future revision efforts. By documenting both settled issues and open disagreements, it helps future standards bodies understand the reasoning behind current requirements and where evolution should occur.
sections.eli5: This document shows how real Internet experts argue about and decide on computer rules, and it helps future experts understand what worked and what still needs fixing.
